strengths: The method can be applied to various Text-to-Video models, clearly stating the intended goal of simultaneously editing the content's motion and appearance.
The paper presents results applied to multiple Text-to-Video models. Experiments using various prompts demonstrate that this method is not limited to specific prompts.
The video quality available on the project page is excellent, and the experimental results are easy to understand.
Videos generated using UniEdit outperformed existing methods in terms of CLIP score, Frame Quality, and Temporal Quality.

Unified Framework for Motion and Appearance Editing: UniEdit effectively addresses a key challenge in video editing by providing a single framework that can handle both motion and appearance modifications. This is achieved by leveraging the inherent properties of spatial and temporal self-attention layers in the T2V model. The motion-reference branch, conditioned on the target prompt, injects motion features into the temporal self-attention layers, enabling text-guided motion changes. The reconstruction branch focuses on preserving source content by injecting features into the spatial self-attention layers.

Zero-Shot Editing Capability: UniEdit operates in a tuning-free manner, meaning it doesn't require fine-tuning the base T2V model for each new video or editing task. This makes it highly efficient and user-friendly, as it avoids the computational cost and complexity associated with model training.

Emphasis on Temporal Consistency: Maintaining temporal consistency is crucial for high-quality video editing. UniEdit tackles this challenge by injecting features from the reconstruction branch into the spatial self-attention layers, which helps preserve the content and structure of the source video. The use of mask-guided coordination further enhances the consistency of unedited areas.
The paper demonstrates good clarity in writing, making it easy for readers to follow the flow of ideas.
The paper is well-motivated, offering various types of video editing while preserving non-target properties using a unified framework.
The design of attention replacement for appearance, structure, and motion editing is technically sound, leveraging the insights and functionality of spatial and temporal self-attention, respectively.
The paper and the auxiliary material show impressive editing results produced with their framework with substantial improvement on existing baselines, especially in temporal coherence.

In this work, they present UniEdit, a tuning-free framework that supports both video motion and appearance editing by harnessing the power of a pre-trained text-to-video generator within an inversionthen-generation framework. To realize motion editing while preserving source video content, based on the insights that temporal and spatial self-attention layers encode inter-frame and intra-frame dependency respectively, they introduce auxiliary motion-reference and reconstruction branches to produce text-guided motion and source features respectively. The obtained features are then injected into the main editing path via temporal and spatial self-attention layers.
weaknesses: The user study involved only 10 participants, which may lead to highly subjective results. Including subjective results in the main performance table could confuse readers, and it would be beneficial to either evaluate with more participants or clearly indicate near the table that the results may be subjective due to the limited number of participants.
The approach of injecting motion text seems like a minor modification rather than a significant technical breakthrough.
Compared to existing methods that inject optical flow information or motion trajectories, it is unclear if providing a motion prompt offers greater control in practice.

The contribution appears to rely on manipulating spatial-temporal attention—a concept already widely explored in video editing—using a slightly modified approach, raising questions about its originality and its position within the broader landscape of video editing research.
16 frames are too short to demonstrate practical utility, especially for long video editing tasks; addressing this limitation would significantly enhance the impact and applicability of the method.

While the emphasis on being tuning-free is appreciated, the limitations imposed by the baseline, particularly in extending the method to editability and long video generation, suggest that incorporating a fine-tuned model might be necessary; additionally, the spatial and temporal attention mechanisms have become standard, and adopting more advanced, fine-tuning-based methods such as ReVideo seems necessary to achieve broader applicability.

The problem is challenging, and the paper only partially addresses it; the editing capabilities need to be more clearly defined, and it is practically impossible to guarantee success for every possible textual input.
Specify the categories of motion and appearance edits that UniEdit is designed to handle effectively.
Provide guidelines or examples of text prompts that might pose challenges for UniEdit, particularly those involving complex scenes or multiple simultaneous edits.
Discuss specific scenarios where UniEdit is known to perform poorly, offering insights into the reasons for these limitations.
UniEdit's core techniques are not entirely novel and are inspired by existing approaches such as auxiliary branches, feature injection via self-attention, and temporal and spatial self-attention.
The improvements, while statistically significant, do not represent a leap in performance but rather a modest refinement of existing techniques, with only 1-2% improvement in some metrics.
UniEdit has a performance ceiling when performing both motion and appearance editing simultaneously and struggles with complex scenes.
Missing critical baseline: ReVideo should be included as a baseline for comparison.
Additional related works such as AnyV2V, I2VEdit, and FLATTEN are not compared, limiting the evaluation.
The evaluation relies heavily on CLIP scores and user preferences; the absence of more comprehensive metrics limits the robustness of the evaluation.
The evaluation dataset could include BalanceCC.
The quantitative analysis shows that the choice of injection steps influences the quality and consistency of the output.
The qualitative exploration indicates a trade-off between stylization and fidelity controlled by the blend layers and steps, suggesting a need for adjustment based on the desired outcome.
The related works are organized by broad topics rather than specific innovations, making it harder to discern how UniEdit differentiates itself from existing methods.

The authors claim better tackle source video with large dynamics, but most visual examples are with small motion magnitudes, and temporal inconsistencies are noticeable in videos with large motion, suggesting the method struggles with significant motion changes.

The claim that UniEdit is not limited to specific video diffusion models is inaccurate because the framework depends on separate spatial and temporal attention design and is incompatible with full 3D attention models, limiting general applicability.
The reliance on the inversion-and-generation paradigm may perform better on generated videos but struggles with out-of-domain real videos, raising questions about robustness and generalizability.
Motion-editing results show background changes, indicating a lack of precise control over editing, where changes intended for the foreground affect the background.

The user study involved an insufficient number of participants (only 10), making it difficult to support the conclusions effectively with robust experimental results; a larger, more diverse participant pool would be necessary.
Using ReferenceNet is not a novel approach in video generation; the difference between this work and previous work is unclear.
The paper overclaims that UniEdit represents a pioneering leap in text-guided, tuning-free video motion editing without sufficient justification.
Lack of comparison: many new works such as Revideo, COVE, accepted by NeurIPS 2024, are not included in this paper.
All results are only 16 frames, which is too short for long video editing.
Motion editing appears to produce similar motions; the method's ability to edit motion is unclear.
Inconsistency issues such as the cat-to-dog example where the head turn consistency is problematic and exhibits sudden changes.
